clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia distinguished by a prominent sensory axonal neuropathy, so areflexia and loss of vibration and joint-position sense accompany gait and limb ataxia.
Caused by an expanded GGC (polyglycine-encoding) repeat in ZFHX3 on chromosome 16q22.1 — the same cytogenetic band as SCA31, from which it must be separated by molecular testing.
Usually presents in mid-adult life with slowly progressive gait unsteadiness; the phenotype was originally delineated in a large Utah kindred of Scandinavian ancestry.
The neuropathy is length-dependent and axonal, with reduced or absent sensory nerve action potentials and relatively preserved motor conduction.
Pyramidal signs such as extensor plantar responses may coexist with the peripheral sensory loss, giving a mixed central-peripheral picture.
Oculomotor abnormalities, particularly gaze-evoked nystagmus, are common, whereas cognition is generally preserved.
Anticipation across generations may be observed, in keeping with an unstable expanded repeat.
reference.pathophysiology: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 4 is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder attributed to an expanded GGC (polyglycine-encoding) repeat within the ZFHX3 gene at chromosome 16q22.1. ZFHX3 encodes a large zinc-finger homeobox transcription factor, and the pathogenic expansion is thought to generate a toxic polyglycine-containing protein with intranuclear inclusions, driving degeneration of cerebellar Purkinje cells together with dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons and their central and peripheral projections. This combined cerebellar and sensory ganglionopathy explains the characteristic pairing of progressive ataxia with a length-dependent axonal sensory neuropathy. Although the locus lies in the same chromosomal band as SCA31, the two disorders arise from different repeat expansions in different genes and are clinically and genetically distinct.
additionalDifferentials: SCA31 (shares the 16q22 region but tends to cause a purer, later-onset cerebellar ataxia)
SCA25 (dominant ataxia with prominent sensory neuronopathy, linked to PNPT1 on chromosome 2p)
SCA18 (sensorimotor neuropathy with ataxia, with added motor weakness and atrophy)
Friedreich ataxia (recessive, with sensory neuropathy, areflexia and cardiomyopathy)
CANVAS — cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome (RFC1 biallelic expansion)
Acquired sensory neuronopathy (paraneoplastic anti-Hu, Sjogren-related ganglionopathy)
Vitamin E deficiency and ataxia with vitamin E deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Targeted molecular testing for the ZFHX3 repeat expansion using repeat-primed or long-range assays
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to characterise the axonal sensory neuropathy
MRI brain demonstrating cerebellar and often vermian atrophy
Broader hereditary-ataxia or repeat-expansion gene panel to exclude sibling subtypes
Quantitative sensory testing and formal assessment of proprioception
Bloods to exclude acquired sensory neuropathy (vitamin B12, glucose and glycated haemoglobin, autoimmune and paraneoplastic screen)
Family pedigree analysis with genetic counselling where appropriate
redFlags: Rapidly progressive ataxia or subacute sensory neuronopathy suggesting a paraneoplastic or autoimmune rather than hereditary cause.
New bulbar dysfunction with dysphagia and aspiration risk.
Severe proprioceptive loss producing frequent falls and injury.
Cardiac or autonomic symptoms that should prompt reconsideration of Friedreich ataxia.
reference.prognosis: Typically slowly progressive over decades with lifespan preserved in most patients; disability arises from the combination of cerebellar incoordination and sensory loss, often leading to reliance on walking aids in later life.
pitfalls: Attributing the ataxia solely to cerebellar disease and overlooking the defining sensory neuropathy.
Confusing SCA4 with SCA31 because both map to 16q22 — molecular confirmation of the specific gene is essential.
Assuming a negative common panel excludes the diagnosis when the ZFHX3 expansion requires a dedicated repeat assay.
Mislabelling an acquired sensory ganglionopathy as hereditary in the absence of a clear dominant family history.
